title: He must increase (John 3:22–30)
hook: John the Baptist rejoices to become less

segments.voice: Yesterday, John 3:16 off the poster: God so loved the world, this world, by giving. Your line was so loved the world. Did a hard headline get that answer? Day four hundred ninety-nine.

You started something. A band, a small business, a ministry at church, a club at school. It grew because of you. And then someone new shows up, and they're better at it, and people start following them instead. Your friends come to you, upset on your behalf: did you see? Everyone's going over there now. Most of us know the little sting in that moment. Today John the Baptist's disciples bring him exactly that news, about the man he baptized in the Jordan, and his answer is one of the most surprising things anyone says in this Gospel.
screen: `YOU STARTED SOMETHING.` → `SOMEONE NEW DOES IT BETTER.` → `EVERYONE IS GOING OVER THERE.`

segments.voice: Jesus and his disciples are baptizing in Judea, and John is still baptizing nearby. John's disciples come to him: Rabbi, the one who was with you across the Jordan, the one you pointed out, he's baptizing, and all men come to him. You can hear the worry in it. John answers first with a principle, in the Douay-Rheims: "A man cannot receive any thing, unless it be given him from heaven." Whatever we have is given. Then a picture from a wedding. The bride belongs to the bridegroom. The bridegroom's friend, the best man, doesn't sulk because the bride isn't his. He stands near, he hears the bridegroom's voice, and he's glad. This, John says, is my joy, and it is full. And then the line: "He must increase, but I must decrease." Must. It isn't a resigned sigh. In John's mouth it sounds like a plan, even a delight. Saint Augustine noticed something about the calendar. The Church celebrates John's birth on June twenty-fourth, just after the longest day of the year, when the daylight starts to shrink. It celebrates Jesus's birth in late December, just after the shortest day, when the light begins to grow. Augustine said the calendar itself preaches this verse: John's days decrease, Christ's increase. The Church doesn't claim the dates were chosen for that reason alone, but Augustine wasn't the last to love the fit. For an ordinary week, the line is a gift. Not every good thing has to have your name on it. Sometimes the best thing you can do for something you love is to step aside and be glad.
screen: `ALL MEN COME TO HIM.` · `NOTHING UNLESS GIVEN FROM HEAVEN.` · `THE BRIDEGROOM'S FRIEND REJOICES.` · `JUNE AND DECEMBER.` · then, large: `HE MUST INCREASE, BUT I MUST DECREASE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone else the credit. Settle, and breathe. Think of a recent win you were part of. A project, a family dinner, a team result. Now find the person whose part got less notice than yours. Picture what they did. Let yourself be glad about it, the way the bridegroom's friend is glad, not grudging. Plan exactly how you'll name it: a message, a sentence in a meeting, a word at the table. If you pray, you can thank God for them. The bell holds the time.
He must increase. John the Baptist's joyful answer when the crowds left him for Jesus: he must increase, but I must decrease. Today's word.
Your line: he must increase. Today, give someone else the credit out loud, and see if you can be glad about it. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist on June 24 and Christmas on December 25, and preachers have long linked the two dates to John's words, he must increase, but I must decrease.

original.note: Latin, from the Vulgate of John 3:30: he must increase. The line Augustine tied to the calendar.

trapdoor: what you thought: John was being modest, or giving up.
what it means: John rejoices to step aside, like the best man glad at the bridegroom's voice.
what a scholar hears: Augustine noted John's feast falls as daylight begins to shorten and Christmas as it begins to grow; the dates' origins are debated.

notes: Augustine's link between the solstices and John 3:30: found in his sermons for the Nativity of John the Baptist (e.g., Sermon 287; also 194, 380). Confirm the citation.
The origins of the December 25 and June 24 dates are debated; the voice says the Church doesn't claim they were chosen for that reason alone. Confirm.
June 24 falls a few days after the solstice; 'just after the longest day' is approximate. Confirm.
Original: Vulgate 'Illum oportet crescere, me autem minui'. Ecclesiastical pronunciation of 'crescere' is approximately KRESH-eh-reh. Confirm.
